header.title: Pro Fide Catholica Adversus Pintam Episcopum Arianum Liber Unus: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Fulgentius Ruspensis Episcopus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's stoa0128b.stoa013.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0128b.stoa013.opp-l: Line 1 (§1): the sentence beginning 'This principle…' is awkwardly constructed in the Latin and may be corrupt; translated literally. §2: 'ad ritum facilius' is obscure and possibly corrupt; translated loosely as 'to convey more easily'. 'Valentinianistae a Valente' presumably means Valentinus; the text says Valens. Some biblical references corrected from evident scanning errors (John 10:30 for x, 50; Deut. 32:39 for 59). §3: the edition notes that a word ('conventus', council) seems to be missing after 'Ariminensis'; supplied in brackets. §4: 'sine ulla oneris jactura' ('without any loss of burden') is obscure. The conditional 'For if the Catholic mother received…' lacks a main clause in the Latin. §5: 'Interroga Patris quae honorificentia' seems defective (a footnote mark follows), so the sense is uncertain. Psalm and Kings references follow the Vulgate numbering.

The text's references are sometimes wrong or garbled and have been given in corrected form: 'Coloss. x, 27' is Col. 1:27; '1 Tim. v, 14' is 1 Tim. 6:14–15; the verse cited 'to the Philippians, in the same' is in fact 1 Thess. 3:11; 'Zach. it' is Zech. 2. The Apocalypse quotation at the end conflates Rev. 3:14 and 1:8. 'Si de Patre accipitur, visibilis erit' (Heb. 6:13) is obscure; the sense seems to be that if the swearing God is the Father, he would have to be visible. 'locutus sum vos' is read as 'locutus sum ad vos'. 'Joannes ad Parthos' is the traditional Latin title for 1 John. In the closing sentence 'Movet ... moveat' is rendered as 'It troubles [them] ... let it trouble [them]'. The paragraph number 'i.' is read as 7, following 6 and the next section's 8.

Line 9: 1 John 5:7 is the 'Johannine Comma', absent from the early Greek manuscripts; it is translated as this text gives it. Several scriptural references in the edition are misprinted or scanned wrongly and have been corrected silently where evident (e.g. John 3:34 for 'III, 31', Wis. 1:3–5, 2 Thess. 2:13, 2 Cor. 3:3, 1 John 3:24, 2 Pet. 1:20–21). Embedded page numbers (541–544) and the stray 'a' before 'corroborari' are omitted. Line 10: 'in obedientium gentium' read as 'in obedientiam gentium'. The quotation of John 6:62 ('If then you see the Son of Man ascending...') stands incomplete in the text. 'Nullus liber nisi Deus, quod est Spiritus sanctus' is rendered literally; the sense is that only God is free, and the Spirit is God. 'Joannis ad Parthos' is the traditional Latin title for 1 John.

Much of this passage closely follows Gregory of Nazianzus (in Rufinus's Latin) and Augustine; 'non factus ex Patre ante saecula' read as printed, though the sense seems to require 'not made, [but begotten] of the Father'. The sentence 'Qui in coelo ... præbet exemplum' is grammatically loose; the number 545 is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted. Read 'vita et vivificans' for 'vita est, et vivificans' (light and enlightening), per the parallel structure.

nodes.text: SAINT FULGENTIUS: ON BEHALF OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH, AGAINST PINTA, THE ARIAN BISHOP. ONE BOOK.

1. That, after Christ, the apostles are the most faithful foundation of the Catholic faith, the sure integrity of the faith bears witness. This principle, even if preaching itself should perhaps cease, some hidden working of the Holy Spirit, sown and grown firm in the minds of the faithful, instils. Yet who among right believers does not know that all heresies have gone out from the Catholic [Church], like useless branches cast off from the vine? But she herself remains in her root, in her vine, in her charity, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against her (Matt. 16:18). The one Church, the true Church, the Catholic Church, fighting against all heresies, can fight, but cannot be conquered. Of her Solomon speaks in the Song of Songs, in the person of Christ praising his bride, whom we believe to be the Church: Behold, my neighbour is like a lily among thorns (Song 2:2). For her integrity is pricked daily by the doctrines of various heresies as if by thorns, so that she may be exercised in watchfulness against her enemies, until, standing out like a lily on the head of her bridegroom, she is adorned with that very whiteness.

2. But since a certain man, driven by his own spirit, has presumed that the followers of this faith should be called Homoousians or Unisubstantialists, his ignorance must be answered. For so great and of such a kind is almighty God that he proclaims good things even through bad men; just as through a wicked high priest (John 11:49) he deigned to foretell the mystery of our redemption. For the man who composed this booklet, conceived in a savage mind, thought fit to set a heap of divine testimonies, from both the New and the Old Testament, against the *homoousion*. Of such men the Apostle long ago foretold, saying: Understanding neither what they say, nor the things about which they make assertions (1 Tim. 1:7). For if he knew what *homoousion* expresses when rendered from Greek into Latin, he would strive to praise it rather than to reproach it. For our three hundred and eighteen Fathers, who prepared the antidote of this word to shut out the poisons of Arius, did not use words foreign to the Gospel, but took care, word for word, to convey more easily the principle of the right faith to those who did not yet understand it. For in the Greek language *homos* means 'one' and *usia* 'substance'. Consult the saying of the Gospel, and you will find this uttered by the divine mouth: I and the Father are one (John 10:30). Examine the plural, and return to the singular truth of the substance. For when he said, I and the Father are one, by saying 'are' he pronounced judgement on the Father's person and his own against Sabellius, whom he foresaw as a heretic to come, so as to distinguish his own person and the Father's. When he said 'one', he likewise foresaw Arius, who does not hesitate to cut apart the substance of the Godhead. For Sabellius wrongly joined, and Arius more wickedly separated. Sabellius ought to have distinguished the person of the Father and of the Son, and Arius ought not to have separated the substance of the Godhead in any way at all. They think indeed that a great charge is laid upon the Catholic faith when they call its nurslings Homoousians or Unisubstantialists, as if *homoousion*, or the substance of the Godhead, contained the name of some man; just as the founders of the various heresies thought that the sect bearing their own name should be preached to their disciples. Thus the Simonians from Simon, the Menandrians from Menander, the Marcionites from Marcion, the Valentinians from Valens, the Manichaeans from Mani, the Nepotians from Nepos; and, to pass over the ancient heresies that are now almost dying out, I shall name meanwhile the recent ones: such as the Sabellians from Sabellius, the Arians from Arius, the Eunomians from Eunomius, the Macedonians from Macedonius, the Apollinarists from Apollinaris, the Nestorians from Nestorius, the Donatists from Donatus, the Maximianists from Maximian, the Rogatists from Rogatus; and any others there are who are called Christians in name only, not in deed, who, having abandoned God, revere the names of their founders. Let him who thought the *homoousion* should be charged against the Catholics show that *homoousion* is the name of some man. For it would seem to me that, had not the most bright summit of the Gospel become known to all nations clearer than light, the Arians, in the way they thought their heresy should be fostered, could have rooted out of the Gospel the very words of the Lord, that is, I and the Father are one; which (as has been said), translated word for word, the Fathers established as *homoousion*.

3. As for what they assert among the ignorant, whether many or few ought to be believed, on the ground that the Council of Nicaea was held with three hundred and eighteen Fathers, whereas they boast that the [Council] of Ariminum was assembled with eight hundred and thirty, where crafty men tried among the ignorant to tamper with the *homoousion*, I shall report briefly. See, the *homoousion* prevailed among a few, in such a way that it became known to the other bishops established throughout the expanses of the whole world, so that they rejoice to be adorned with its confession. But if the later [council] of Ariminum was assembled in so great a multitude, as they assert, the bishops of that sect would have multiplied throughout the world, its peoples would have grown, and such a faith would have taken hold even of the empires themselves. But once the craftiness of that fraud was recognised by prudent and most approved men, the *homoousion* was so confirmed that we see scarcely any remnants of Ariminum left to test the Catholics. Let us consult, if you please, the very city of Ariminum, where this business of fraud was carried out, or rather contrived. Whether it has a bishop of that sect I do not know; but about Milan I may assert more freely, where Auxentius, like a crafty craftsman, poured out the poisons of his sect. His successor Ambrose, filled with the Holy Spirit, so destroyed his doctrine that after his death his name was erased from the memory of the living in that very city, and his name is held as a kind of contagion. Through this Ambrose the faith of the then Emperor Gratian was also strengthened, and its increases among bishops and peoples grew more and more. For almighty God, who through all the Scriptures promised increases to his Church, could not abandon his promise and allow falsehood to grow. Let this be said about all heresies.

4. Furthermore, in what follows, with the help of God, who both instructs the heart and governs the tongue, testimonies will be set out concerning the one God, and the power, invisibility and equality of the Son with the Father, and the Godhead of the Holy Spirit, which Trinity, even against their will, is nevertheless one God; such testimonies that, if they do not love the darkness of contention, they must see the light of truth. And lest anyone be troubled that we said increases were promised to the Church through all the Scriptures, if they claim that [increases] have been granted [to them] through this oppression, let them know that it is written in Jeremiah: The partridge will cry out, it will gather those it did not hatch, it will make its riches not with judgement (Jer. 17:11). And this is the most certain proof that the Catholic faith has never grown except through tribulations and persecutions, so that what was said may be fulfilled: For through many tribulations and hardships we must see the kingdom of God (Acts 14:21). But the increases of that [other] faith are attested by the exiles of the innocent, the proscriptions of the wretched, and the torments and oppression of captives. But I see certain opponents in labour [with objections], and casting up at us the persecutions of the Donatists, whose fury did violence to the laws, and who suffered these things by the laws. For if the Catholic mother received any of them into her loving bosom, [it was] without any injury to baptism, without any loss of burden, without any insult to the Holy Spirit, so that those who were converted willingly grieved that charity had long been hidden from them.
Catholic testimonies concerning the one God.

5. The first word of God: Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God (Deut. 6:4). In Deuteronomy: The Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign god with them (Deut. 32:12). Likewise there: See, see that I am God, and there is no other besides me (ibid., 39). Likewise in Exodus: You shall have no other gods besides me (Exod. 20:3). Likewise: He who sacrifices to other gods besides me shall be rooted out (ibid., 5). Likewise: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve (Deut. 6:13). Likewise: For there is no other God either in heaven or on earth who can do your works, or be compared to your greatness (Deut. 3:24). In the prophet Hosea: You shall know no Lord besides me, and there shall be no saviour besides me (Hos. 13:4). In Isaiah: I am God, and there is no saviour besides me: I have announced, and I have saved, and there shall be no foreign [god] among you (Isa. 43:11). The same as above: Thus says the Lord, who made heaven; this is God who stretched out the earth and made it: he did not make it in vain, but that it might be inhabited. I am, I am, and there is no other. I am God, and there is no other (Isa. 45:18). By myself I swear, righteousness shall go forth from my mouth, my words shall not return: for to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear by God (ibid., 22, 23 and 24). The same as above: From of old we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen, a God besides you (Isa. 64:4); and: Before me there was no God, and after me there shall be no other (Isa. 43:10). I am God the first, and I am in the things that come after (Isa. 44:6). In the body of the Psalms: Who is God but our Lord (Ps. 17:32)? Likewise: What god is great like our God? You are the God who alone does wonders (Ps. 76:15). Likewise: Let the nations know that your name is Lord: you alone are most high over all the earth (Ps. 82:16). This applies rather to the Son. In [the Books of] Kingdoms, Hezekiah against Sennacherib: O Lord God of Israel, you alone are God of all the kings of the earth (4 Kgs 19:15). The same as above: O Lord our God, save us from their hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the Lord (ibid., 19). Solomon in prayer spread out his hands towards heaven and said: O Lord God of Israel, there is no God like you, neither in heaven above nor on earth beneath (3 Kgs 8:23). And although two or three testimonies concerning the one God would suffice, let those nevertheless hear who bring in two gods upon us. For they confess God the Father and God the Son: this is indeed true; but whoever does not honour the Son as he honours the Father is impious. For if sacrifice or honour is owed to the Father, it is owed also to the Son. But when you assert that the Father is greater and the Son lesser, you bring in two gods: you are sacrilegious on both counts, both in not hearing, The Lord your God is one God (Deut. 6:4), and in not honouring the Son as you honour the Father. The Son set no degrees between [them]. Ask what honour [is due] to the Father. You strive to insult both: the Father, because his Son is not heard, of whom the Father says, Hear him (Matt. 17:5); and the Son, whom you dare to despise in his own command. But now let other testimonies concerning the equality of the Father and the Son be set forth.
Testimonies concerning the equality of the Father and the Son.

6. In the Apocalypse: And he had written on his garment, or on his thigh, King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16; 1 Tim. 6:15). If the Apostle says this of the Father, here it is plainly said of the Son. In the same book: Blessed and holy is he who has a part in the first resurrection. Over them the second death has no power; but they will be priests of God and of his Christ, and will reign with him (Rev. 20:6). In the same book: I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life freely. He who conquers will possess these things, and I will be his God, and he will be my son (Rev. 21:6[–7]). In the same book: And I saw no temple in it. For the Lord God almighty is its temple, and the Lamb (ibid. 22). No difference. In the same book: And he showed me a river of the water of life, shining, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb (Rev. 22:1). One throne, not two. In the same book: The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and they will serve him (ibid. 3). In the Epistle of John: Everyone who does not abide in the teaching of Christ does not have God. He who abides in the teaching has both the Son and the Father (2 John 9). The Son first. In the Epistle of Jude: Denying our Master and God, Jesus Christ (Jude 4). Both God and Lord. In the Apocalypse: They say to the mountains and rocks, Hide us from the face of him who sits on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who will be able to stand? (Rev. 6:16[–17]). One judgement, or an equal one. In the same book: Salvation to our God and to the Lamb (Rev. 7:10). In the same book: The kingdom of this world has become [the kingdom] of the Lord our God and of his Christ, and he will reign for ever and ever (Rev. 11:15). He will reign, not They will reign. In the same book: And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying, Now have come the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ (Rev. 12:10). No division. In the same book: And I looked, and behold, the Lamb was standing on Mount Zion, and with him a hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads (Rev. 14:1). Does it prejudice [the case] that the Son is named first, where there is one power? In the same book: These were bought from among men, first fruits for God and the Lamb (ibid. 4). In the same book: These will make war with the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (Rev. 17:14). What more does the Father have? Let it be said. To the Hebrews: For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying (Heb. 6:13). If it is understood of the Father, he will be visible; if of the Son, there will be none greater than he. The Father in the Gospel: That all may honour the Son as they honour the Father (John 5:23). And as for his having one who sent him, this sending is not from place to place. For the sun too sends out rays and is not separated from itself. Again: As the Father gives life to the dead, so the Son also gives life to whom he wills (ibid. 21). Behold, the Son, to whom he wills; behold, the Spirit, where he wills. The Son says to Philip: He who sees me sees the Father also (John 14:9). And again: Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? (John 14:11). Behold the equality of the Father and the Son. Again: Father, glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you (John 17:1). Equal power. But these things suffice concerning the equality of the Son with the Father.
Testimonies concerning the Godhead of the Son.

7. In Job: Who alone stretches out the heaven, and walks upon the sea as upon the land (Job 9:8). In Jeremiah: This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him; he found out every way of understanding, and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he was seen on earth, and lived among men (Baruch 3:36–38). Because the person of the Son is expressed here by saying, No other will be reckoned beside him, do we therefore separate the Father from the Godhead? In Isaiah: Egypt is wearied, and the trade of Ethiopia. Many will come to you and will be your servants; and they will walk behind you, bound in fetters; and they will worship you and make supplication to you: for God is in you, and you alone are God, and we did not know it: the God of Israel, our Saviour (Isa. 45:14–15). In this most clear testimony not only the Godhead of the Son is shown, but also his supreme equality with the Father. For what he says, God is in you, and you are God, is what is said in the Gospel: I am in the Father, and the Father is in me (John 14:11). To the Romans: Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever (Rom. 9:5). The Godhead proper to the Son. Second to the Corinthians: Who is the image of the invisible God (2 Cor. 4:4). If the image, [then] the truth. In the same: God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19). If God, wholly, not in part. To the Ephesians: To preach the incomprehensible riches of Christ (Eph. 3:8). Are they Christ's alone, and not the Father's? To the Colossians: For in him it pleased all the fullness of the Godhead to dwell bodily (Col. 2:9). Note here that [it says] both all the fullness and the Godhead: where there is nothing that can be added. In the same: That God might show the riches of his mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ (Col. 1:27). Behold, Christ is the riches of God. In the same: That [they may come] to the knowledge of the mystery of God, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:[2–]3). Entire fullness. To the Philippians: Who, though he was established in the form of God (Phil. 2:6). You hear 'form', and you deny [him] equal? In the same: Now may God the Father himself and our Lord Jesus Christ direct our way to you (1 Thess. 3:11). Behold, both direct: equal power. First to Timothy: That you keep the commandment without reproach until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom in his own times the blessed and only Mighty One will show (1 Tim. 6:14[–15]), etc. Because he said, Only Mighty One, is the Father excluded from might? To Titus: The grace of God and of our Saviour Jesus Christ has shone upon all men (Tit. 2:11). In the same (v. 13): Awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ. If the Son is the great God, he has nothing less. In the same: But when the kindness and humanity of our Saviour Jesus Christ shone forth (Tit. 3:4). Here he was silent neither about the humanity nor about the divinity. John to the Parthians: That we may believe in his true Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life (1 John 5:20). In [the face of] this testimony, whoever denies to the Son the perfection of God is Antichrist. Second of Peter: For so an entrance will be richly provided for you into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ (2 Pet. 1:11). And although these few testimonies concerning the Godhead of the Son are like a drop lifted from the great sea of the Scriptures themselves, since all Scripture bears witness both to his Godhead and to his humanity by reason of the flesh he assumed, as he himself says in the Gospel according to John: Search the Scriptures, for you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me (John 5:39). He does not say, About us, so as not to bring in two gods. In Luke Jesus said to them: These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). Does he exclude the Father from the testimony of the Scriptures because here too he says, About me? On the omnipotence of the Son, in Solomon: Your almighty word, O Lord, came from heaven, from the royal thrones (Wis. 18:15). In Zechariah: O, flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for I will gather you from the four winds of heaven. The Lord says: Be saved in Zion, you who dwell in the daughter of Babylon. Therefore thus says the Lord almighty: After glory he has sent me to the nations that plundered you. For whoever touches you is as one who touches the pupil of his eye. Therefore I will bring my hand upon them, and they will be plunder for those who plundered them; and you will know that the Lord almighty has sent me (Zech. 2:6 ff.). Above, the Almighty speaks; below, the Almighty sends: are there then two almighties? The prophet Amos: The Lord who touches the earth and makes it shake, and all who dwell in it will mourn; and it will rise like the river of Egypt; who builds his ascent upon heaven, and establishes his descent upon the earth; who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth: the Lord almighty is his name (Amos 9:5[–6]). Are not all these things understood to fit the Son? Who, descending, touched the earth, shook it by his passion, and ascended from earth into heaven, and descended from heaven upon the earth, as he himself promised in the Apocalypse (3:14): Thus says he who is the faithful witness, the beginning of the creation of God: Who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Lord almighty (Rev. 1:8). It troubles [them] that he said, The beginning of the creation of God; let it trouble [them] that it is said, The Lord almighty: so that this refers to the Godhead, and that, that he was born of the Virgin Mary.

8. In the Gospel: Go, baptise the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19). In the name, not in the names. Again: The kingdom of heaven is like a woman who hid leaven in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened (Matt. 13:33). Here the woman stands for the Church, which in equal weights hides the faith of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of believers. In the Apocalypse: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth (Rev. 4:8). Three times I hear 'holy', and one Lord God. In the same place: And the angel said to me: These are the true words of God. And I fell before his feet to worship him; and he said to me: See that you do not do it; I am your fellow servant, and [the fellow servant] of your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus, and the spirit of prophecy (Rev. 19:9–10). What is clearer than light for showing the Trinity, if not the true words of the Father, the testimony of the Son, the gift of prophecy of the Holy Spirit? In the Psalms: With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light (Ps. 35:10). With God the Father is Christ, the fountain of life; and since the light is in him, the Holy Spirit is seen as the one who gives light: for whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his (Rom. 8:9). In Psalm 66:8: May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him. Three times I hear 'God', and it proclaims one to be feared. In the Epistle of John: There are three in heaven who bear witness, the Father, the Word, and the Spirit: and the three are one (1 John 5:7). What shall I say of the patriarch Abraham? When he saw the form of three men, he recognised one God in them, when he says: Lord and Master (Gen. 18:3). By bodily service he shows the duty of hospitality to three; yet from one he received the blessing of offspring, when it is said to him: At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son (v. 10). He did not say 'we will come', but 'I will come', so as not to seem to introduce a crowd of gods. For that you may know that the Trinity dwells together, and together shuns impurity, hear what the Lord says in the Gospel: He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him (John 14:21); and, We will come, I and my Father, and make our dwelling with him (v. 23). Behold, the Father and the Son inhabit one dwelling. What of the Holy Spirit? Hear the Apostle saying: You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you (1 Cor. 3:16). It has been shown that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit dwell together; let it be shown that the Trinity itself together shuns impurity. In Solomon you have: But perverse thoughts separate from God: this of the Father. For Wisdom will not enter a malicious soul: this of the Son. For the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding (Wis. 1:3–5): this of the Holy Spirit. But that you may gather, by a shortcut of understanding, the sense of Scripture speaking as one about the nature of the Trinity, you likewise have in Exodus: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob (Exod. 3:6). In the Psalm: The Lord lives, and blessed be my God, and let the God of my salvation be exalted (Ps. 17:47). Paul: The same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God (1 Cor. 12:4–6). Does it offend the Catholic sense that the Spirit is named first? Again, if you ask whether the Trinity itself is called Lord, hear: Bring to the Lord glory and honour, bring to the Lord glory to his name (Ps. 28:2). That the Trinity itself is King: Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory (Ps. 23:9[–10]). The testimony is given: God repeated three times, the Lord three times called King. Neither gods nor lords nor kings are made distinct because they are distinguished into three names and persons: for there is one Godhead, one lordship, one royal rule. Whoever contradicts this truth out of an evil zeal for winning, I do not say will be condemned, but is already condemned.
Testimonies concerning the Holy Spirit, that he is God.

9. At the beginning of the book of Genesis: And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters (Gen. 1:2): one who would sanctify the waters as a figure of baptism, not one who would rest from weariness. In Job: It is the divine Spirit who made me, and the Spirit of the Almighty who teaches me (Job 33:4). Perfection in divinity. In the Gospel: God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (John 4:24). Again: For God does not give the Spirit by measure (John 3:34). Behold, the Spirit is immeasurable. To Nicodemus: For the Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, and do not know where he comes from or where he goes (ibid. 8). When you hear 'where he wills', it is his own power. Christ of himself: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me (Luke 4:18). Unless a pious understanding recalls these words [to their right sense], the Spirit will be greater than the Son. Again: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan (ibid. 1). The same understanding [applies]. Again: If then you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before. It is the Spirit who gives life: for the flesh profits nothing (John 6:[62–]63). He who gives life has nothing less of Godhead. Again: When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth, whom the Father will send in my name, he will lead you into all truth, and will teach you (John 16:13). It is God who will lead into all truth. In the Acts of the Apostles, Peter to Cornelius: Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit (Acts 10:38). The man was anointed, not God. Again to Ananias: Why has Satan tempted your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:3)? And he adds: You have not lied to men, but to God (v. 4). Again: Thus says the Holy Spirit: Set apart for me Saul and Barnabas, for the ministry to which I have called them (Acts 13:2). Here he brings in the person neither of the Father nor of the Son, yet a sound understanding does not separate them from the command. Again the Apostle to the Gentiles by letter: It has seemed good, he says, to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no more than that you abstain from idols, from fornication, and from blood (Acts 15:28). Was this command made without the Father and the Son? Again there: And the Spirit said to Peter: Rise and go with them, for I have sent them to you (Acts 10:19[–20]). Who but the Creator gives orders to the creature? Again there: From Miletus Paul sent to Ephesus and called together the presbyters and elders (Acts 20:17); and after much exhortation he added: Take heed to the flock of Christ, over which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops (ibid. 28). Is the Father or the Son separated from this appointment of a priest? Paul to the Romans: But the Spirit is eternal life and peace (Rom. 8:6). This the Father is, this the Son, this the Holy Spirit; but one life, not three. In the same place: The Spirit is life because of righteousness (ibid. 10). This the Father is, this the Son. In the same place: But if the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you (v. 11). What kind of God is this, who raised the flesh of the Creator from the dead? In the same place: For we have not received the spirit of slavery (v. 15). No one is free except God, which the Holy Spirit is. In the same place: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing: in abundance of hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit (Rom. 15:13). As Christ is the power of God, so is the Holy Spirit. In the same place: That the offering of the Gentiles may be made sanctified in the Holy Spirit (ibid. 16). As the Spirit gives life, so he also sanctifies. In the same place: For I do not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not worked through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed; by the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit (ibid. 18–19). The Son is power, the Spirit is power, the Father is power; but one, not three. First to the Corinthians: But the Spirit searches all things. No one knows the things of God except his Spirit (1 Cor. 2:10–11). In the same place: You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you (1 Cor. 3:16). It is God who dwells in his temple. In the same place: You have been washed and sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Spirit of our God (1 Cor. 6:11). Behold, the Son and the Holy Spirit together cleanse, together sanctify. In the same place: One and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11). He who freely does what he wills is subject to no one. Second to the Corinthians: A letter written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God (2 Cor. 3:3). A man's spirit is not less than the man; how much more the Spirit of God! In the same place: The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (ibid. 6). He who gives life is God: for the Lord kills and gives life (1 Kgs [1 Sam.] 2:6). To the Galatians: That we may receive the blessing of the Spirit through faith (Gal. 3:14). It is God who blesses. In the same place: If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit (Gal. 5:25). He who blesses, again, himself gives life as God. In the same place: He who sows in the Spirit will reap from the Spirit eternal life (Gal. 6:8). In these three testimonies to the Galatians the Spirit both blesses, and gives life, and gives eternal life. To the Ephesians: In whom, believing, you were sealed in the Holy Spirit (Eph. 1:13). We are sealed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. In the same place: In whom you are built into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit (Eph. 2:22). Again: It has been revealed to his holy apostles in the Spirit that the Gentiles are fellow heirs (Eph. 3:5[–6]). One and the same Spirit works all things: he makes heirs. In the same place: That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit (ibid. 16). None but God strengthens. In the same place: Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3). Christ is peace. Are there two peaces? In the same place: And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6:17). Christ is the word of God; the Holy Spirit is the word of God. Are there two words? To the Philippians: Or, being absent, I may hear of you that you stand in one Spirit (Phil. 1:27), that is, in God. To the Thessalonians: God chose you from the beginning for salvation in the sanctification of the Spirit (2 Thess. 2:13). First to Timothy: Great is the mystery of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit (1 Tim. 3:16). Behold, the Holy Spirit sanctifies even the incarnation of Christ. Second to Timothy: Guard the good deposit entrusted to you, through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us (2 Tim. 1:14). If the Spirit were not God, the Apostle would not dare to adjure his disciple by him. Moreover: who dwells in us. To Titus: He saved us through the washing of regeneration, through the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5). Peter to the Gentiles: They have been announced to you by those who preached the gospel to you, the Holy Spirit being sent from heaven: into which the angels long to look (1 Pet. 1:12). It is God whom the angels long to look upon. In the same place: Christ died for our sins, the just for the unjust, that he might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit (1 Pet. 3:18). In the same place: That they may be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the Spirit (1 Pet. 4:6). In the same place: If you are reproached in Christ, [you are blessed,] because the Spirit of the glory of the Lord rests upon you (ibid. 14). Christ is the glory of the Father; the Holy Spirit is glory. Are there two glories? Second of Peter: Understanding this first, that no prophecy of Scripture comes about by private interpretation. For prophecy was never brought by human will, but men of God spoke moved by the Holy Spirit (2 Pet. 1:20–21). None but God inspires anyone with the gift of prophecy. John to the Parthians: By this we know that he abides in us, by the Holy Spirit whom he has given us (1 John 3:24). In the same place: That we abide in him, and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit (1 John 4:13). 'He has given', as you hear, is an operation of power, not a separation of Godhead. In the Apocalypse: And after three days and a half the Spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet (Rev. 11:11). What proceeds from God is God. In the same place: Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From now on, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours (Rev. 14:13). He did not say the Father, he did not say the Son, but the Spirit, who by this command is shown to be God. To the Hebrews: For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled, sanctify the defiled for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God (Heb. 9:13–14)! This testimony teaches of what power the Holy Spirit is, through whom the flesh of Christ is presented without blemish. In the same place: Anyone who makes void the law of Moses dies without any mercy on the word of two or three witnesses: how much worse punishment do you think he deserves who has trampled on the Son of God, and held the blood of the Covenant unclean, and insulted the Spirit of grace (Heb. 10:28–29)! Behold what kind of vengeance [there is] for injury to the Son and the Holy Spirit. In the same place: God the judge of all, and the spirits of the just made perfect, and Jesus Christ the mediator of the New Covenant (Heb. 12:23[–24]). This testimony fits the Trinity, since the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are named here. That the Holy Spirit is almighty, in Solomon: The Holy Spirit, manifold, subtle, eloquent, sure, undefiled, having all power (Wis. 7:22[–23]). And do you deny that he is almighty? That the Holy Spirit is judge, the Lord says: If I go away, I will send him to you; and when he comes, he will convict the world of sin, of righteousness and of judgement (John 16:7–8). You see a judge who, if it may be said, even vindicates the Saviour himself: and does anyone dare to take Godhead away from him? And what more shall I say of the Godhead of the Holy Spirit, whom David dreads, saying: Where shall I go, Lord, from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your face (Ps. 138:7)? And to conclude: so great and of such a kind is the Holy Spirit that if anyone blasphemes against him, he will find him not forgiving him, neither in this age nor in the age to come.

10. It is impossible to express in human words that ineffable substance or nature of the Divinity: unchangeable, immutable, impassible, simple, uncompounded, indivisible, light unapproachable, power inexplicable, greatness without end, glory that cannot be beheld, goodness to be desired, beauty past searching out, which may indeed touch and move the affection of a pure mind, but cannot be pointed out or explained. There are the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the only nature that is not created, the power of dominion, natural goodness. The Father is the beginning of all things, the cause of all things, the root of the living: from him proceeds the fount of life, the power and unchanged image of the invisible God, who is the Son begotten of the Father, the Word, or living reason; who was always, and was with God, and was God, not made from the Father before the ages, not taken up afterwards or adopted as a son, not by possession or as a thing made, but the creator and maker of all things: who is all that the Father is; to whom the Father, by begetting, gave all that he has. And so, where he who gave, gave by begetting, and he who received, received by being born, it was not a needy one who was helped, but abundance itself that was born. For he who received cannot be unequal to him who gave, since he received this too by being born, that he should be equal. For he has nothing less than the Father who said: All things that the Father has are mine (John 16:15). And because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, not losing the form of God, in that same form of a servant he became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross; in which he was made a little lower than the angels, so that in the form of God he might remain equal; for that form is not changeable. He who in heaven, in the form of God and equal to God, as God offers an example to the pure intellectual spirits, so that he might offer the same example also to fallen man returning, who because of the uncleanness of sins and the penalty of mortality could not see God: he emptied himself, not by losing his divinity but by taking on our humanity; and taking the form of a servant, he came to us into this world, he who was in this world, since the world was made through him (John 1:10), so that he might become an example of God to those who look upward, an example of man to those who wonder below; an example to the healthy for persevering, an example to the sick for recovering; an example to the dying for not fearing, an example to the dead for rising again: himself holding the first place in all things; so that, since man ought to follow nothing but God toward blessedness, and could not perceive God, by following God made man he might at once follow both him whom he could perceive and him whom he ought to follow. Let us therefore love him and cleave to him, by the charity poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. This Spirit is both life and life-giving, light and enlightening; good and goodness; the right Spirit, the princely Spirit, who is Lord of all; sending apostles, setting apart ministers for himself, establishing temples for himself, breathing where he wills, dividing the gifts of the Spirit as he wills. The Spirit of adoption, the Spirit of truth, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of knowledge, of counsel, of power, and of the fear of God: through whom the Father is known and the Son is glorified. For it is not fitting either that the Son was ever lacking to the Father, or the Spirit to the Son: for the divinity would be defrauded in the greatest things, and it would be held as it were inglorious and unworthy, if God had come to the fullness of perfection as if out of repentance and by a belated counsel. Let him who can receive it, receive it (Matt. 19:12); let him who cannot yet, pray that he may receive it, believe that he may receive it: for it is written: Unless you believe, you will not understand (Isa. 7:9, according to the LXX).
